title: Stop Confusing Montessori with Self-Directed Education
author: Katy Purviance
summary: Katy Purviance answers a teacher's question about whether Self-Directed Education is like Montessori by arguing that the two share methods but start from different beliefs about children. She lists genuine overlaps: rejecting grades and testing, trusting children as capable, and using mixed-age groups. The core difference is whether a trained adult should design the environment and sequence of materials, as in Montessori, or whether children already have what they need to learn, as Peter Gray's evolutionary research suggests. She summarizes the evidence honestly: Montessori has strong lottery-based randomized trials and systematic reviews, while evidence for Self-Directed Education rests mainly on self-selected alumni surveys. The post also contrasts Sudbury-style majority voting with sociocratic consent and ends with practical questions for choosing between models.
points: Both models reject grades, standardized testing and reward-punishment systems, but they diverge on who designs the learning environment.
Montessori treats the environment as the curriculum, while Self-Directed Education trusts children's own drives of curiosity, play, sociability and planfulness.
Montessori's research base is notably stronger, including randomized lottery studies, whereas Self-Directed Education relies on self-selected surveys.
Because the Montessori name is not protected, parents should check for accredited guides and the full material sequence.
quotes: Montessori is a theory of the right conditions, built by an adult who has studied where a child should end up. Self-Directed Education is a theory of what children already do when nothing gets in the way.
The two approaches overlap in genuine ways, but they originate from two different beliefs about who a child already is.
Does a child need an adult to design the right environment for them, or does a child already have what they need to learn on their own?
A Montessori child chooses, but she chooses from options an adult has already decided are worth choosing. The environment itself functions as the curriculum.
Democracy decides what most children want. Sociocracy decides what works for every child in the room, which means a single child's objection carries real weight against the whole group.

But these are self-selected surveys, gathered from families who already believe in the model enough to choose it and stay with it. There is no randomized study of Self-Directed Education comparable to the lottery-based Montessori research.

That fidelity question matters, because Montessori was never legally protected as a trademark. Any school can use the name regardless of whether it employs trained guides, complete material sets, or the long uninterrupted work periods the method depends on.
